tip: 'Parliamo' means both 'we talk' and 'let's talk'; same form, and context picks the 'let's talk' reading here.
A negative 'tu' command is 'non' plus the infinitive, not the normal command form: 'non darle il mio numero'.
These conjunctions always trigger the subjunctive: 'prima che' (before), 'senza che' (without), 'a meno che' (unless).
'Per' plus an infinitive expresses purpose, 'in order to': 'per correre' = to run.
'Da' before a person or professional means at or to their place: 'dal medico' = to the doctor's.
'Smettere' links to the next verb with 'di': 'smetta di rimandare' = stop putting things off.
'Bisogna che', meaning one must, takes the subjunctive: 'bisogna che io parli'.
'Vicino' needs 'a' before what it is near: 'vicino al mare' = near the sea.
'Tra' (or 'fra', both fine) before a time span means 'in' for future time: 'tra due anni' = in two years.
'Credo che' (I believe that) takes the subjunctive: 'sia' instead of 'è'.
The 'non' in 'a meno che non cambi' is not a negation; it belongs to 'unless', so this means 'unless I change my mind', not 'unless I don't'.
The informal command of 'dire' shortens to 'di'' with an apostrophe (from 'dici'): 'di' la verità'.
'Ricordati' is 'ricorda' plus 'ti' (yourself): pronouns attach to the end of informal commands.
Negative informal commands use 'non' plus the infinitive: 'non lasciare', never 'non lasci la porta'.
'Stare per' plus an infinitive means to be about to: 'sta per partire' = about to leave.
'Pure' after a command softens it to 'go ahead and': 'inizia pure' = go ahead and start.
'Dovreste' is the conditional of 'dovere', 'you should': soft advice, versus 'dovete', 'you must'.
'Dare una mano', literally 'to give a hand', means to help someone: 'da' una mano a tuo fratello'.
'A voce bassa', literally 'at low voice', means quietly: 'parlate a voce bassa'.
'Prima che' (before) always takes the subjunctive: 'prima che tu decida', not 'decidi'.
Formal commands to 'Lei' use the subjunctive form: 'faccia con calma', not 'fai'.
Object pronouns attach to the end of informal commands: 'prendi' plus 'lo' becomes 'prendilo'.
Hypotheticals pair the conditional with 'se' plus the past subjunctive: 'partirei' (I'd leave), 'se avessi' (if I had).
English drops 'that' in 'the train I take', but 'che' is mandatory in Italian: 'il treno che prendo'.
A past-before-past form marks the earlier of two events: 'era già partito quando siamo arrivati' = it had already left when we arrived.
Singular family members normally drop the article with a possessive: 'tua sorella', not 'la tua sorella'; plurals keep it.
After a preposition you can't use 'che'; one option is preposition plus article plus 'quale': 'con il quale'.
'Dimmi' is the command 'di'' (say) plus 'mi' (me), with the 'm' doubled: pronouns attach to the end of commands.
For '-ere' and '-ire' verbs, the informal 'tu' command matches the present 'tu' form: 'scrivere' gives 'scrivi' (write).
For '-are' verbs, the 'tu' command ends in '-a', not the '-i' of the present: 'guardare' gives 'guarda', not 'guardi'.
